items.question: What does Dizegno do?
items.answer: Dizegno is a branding agency: identity, visual systems, and communication for business. From a logo and guideline to a full brand strategy — depending on what the client actually needs.

items.question: Is it just logos, or more than that?
items.answer: A logo is usually the smallest part of the job. Most projects cover the full visual system — guidelines, typography, packaging, signage — everything a brand needs to stay coherent once it's out in the world.

items.question: What kind of clients do you work with?
items.answer: Mostly banking and fintech, retail, delivery and mobile services, healthcare, automotive, and sports events — from large institutional brands to ambitious early-stage startups. We're open to projects outside this list too, as long as there's something to sink into — a complex system, an interesting market, or a product that has something to say.

items.question: Where are you based?
items.answer: Headquartered in Tashkent, with a multinational team — we bring in strong specialists as needed, including from Russia and the wider region, matched to the scale of the task. Most projects are within the CIS region, but that's more a result of where relationships started than a territorial limit.

items.question: Why choose Dizegno?
items.answer: Dizegno grew from one designer's practice into an agency clients return to — for consistency and craft, not just a portfolio. The team's experience spans banking, automotive, delivery, healthcare, and sports events, meaning there's almost always already a solved problem close to whatever a new client is facing. Every project is curated from brief to delivery, so responsibility never gets diluted across random hands.

items.question: Who is behind Dizegno?
items.answer: Dizegno was founded by Akbar Aminov, who started as an independent designer and gradually grew his practice into an agency. Today the team wins larger briefs on the strength of the work itself, not the size of the roster. Akbar remains the creative director and personally oversees key projects, while a team of specialists — assembled to match the scale of the task — handles delivery.

items.question: Why Dizegno instead of a large international agency or a freelancer?
items.answer: A large international agency gives you a name and scale, but often loses you between an account manager, a strategist, and a designer — responsibility dilutes and speed drops. A freelancer gives you speed and price, but not resilience: no process, no documentation, no backup plan if something goes wrong. Dizegno sits between these two extremes: direct oversight on every project, backed by a process, documentation, and a team that outlasts any single person.

items.question: What makes the process different?
items.answer: There's no handoff between strategy, design, and production — the team that takes on a project carries it through to final files. That continuity is what most studios lose once they scale, and we deliberately keep it as part of how we operate.

items.question: How do you handle confidential information?
items.answer: On request, we sign an NDA before discussing any project details — standard practice for our banking and corporate clients. Some clients appear in our portfolio with restrictions — no public case studies or materials, by agreement only.

items.question: Who owns the rights to the final work?
items.answer: The client — fully, once payment is complete under the contract terms. Source files, guidelines, and all working materials are handed over to the client; we don't retain rights to use the brand after the project ends.

items.question: How long have you been doing this?
items.answer: The team is built around years of experience in branding — at the intersection of identity, packaging, and campaigns, with a focus on industries where consistency and precision matter more than a pretty picture.

items.question: What does a typical project look like, week to week?
items.answer: Discovery and direction first — research and concept work before the first presentation. Then design development in rounds, with a review after each one, until the system is locked. Production and file handoff come last, once everything's approved.

items.question: Do you handle production too — packaging, signage, print files?
items.answer: Yes, through the preparation stage: if the brand needs print-ready packaging dielines, signage specs, or press-ready files, we take them all the way to production-ready, including the technical documentation a printer or contractor needs. The client's production partner or our contractor handles the actual printing and installation — we make sure the files arrive at the shop floor without loss or questions.

items.question: How do projects usually start?
items.answer: With a short conversation. Reach out through the contact page or the button in the corner — describe roughly what you need, and we'll figure out scope and timeline together.

items.question: How quickly do you respond?
items.answer: Promptly — if it's urgent, say so in your message and we'll reply as a priority.

items.question: What should I have ready before reaching out?
items.answer: Nothing formal — a rough sense of the problem is enough. If you already have brand guidelines, past design materials, or a competitor reference you like or dislike, send those too — it saves a round of back-and-forth.

items.question: What if I don't have a brief yet?
items.answer: That's normal, and more common than showing up with a finished brief. Part of the first conversation is turning a vague idea into a working brief — problem, audience, success criteria — before any design work starts.

items.question: Can you work alongside an in-house team or another agency?
items.answer: Regularly. Sometimes we build the whole system from zero, sometimes we're brought in for one piece — a rebrand, a packaging line — that needs to fit inside a larger team's existing process. Both formats work.

items.question: How is pricing structured?
items.answer: Project-based, not hourly — price is tied to scope (number of deliverables, rounds, production work), not time spent. You get a fixed number before anything starts, not an open-ended estimate.

items.question: How long does a typical identity project take?
items.answer: It depends on scope — number of deliverables, depth of production, number of approval rounds. Refreshing an existing mark moves quickly; a full identity system with packaging and signage takes longer. At the start, after a short conversation about the task, we lock in a specific timeline along with the price.
